categories.label: Fragmentation vs Integration under Delivery Method Structures
categories.memo: Covers how the structural characteristics of different project delivery methods (DBB, DB, CM, IPD, EPC, turnkey) affect fragmentation or integration of design and construction responsibilities in MMC/prefabrication projects.

codes.label: DBB Fragmentation Disadvantages MMC
codes.description: Design-Bid-Build separates design from construction, excluding contractors/manufacturers/fabricators from early design input, causing constructability mismatches, slower processes, and disputes in prefabricated/modular projects.

codes.label: Design-Build Consolidation Benefits
codes.description: Design-Build merges design and construction responsibility under one entity, facilitating collaboration and earlier contractor involvement, and is frequently recommended for MMC/prefabrication, though it may still neglect integration of off-site manufacturing.

codes.label: Construction Management as Coordination Mechanism
codes.description: CM delivery is recommended for prefabrication/MiC because it enables enhanced coordination and communication given project technical complexity.

codes.label: Integrated Project Delivery (IPD) as Optimal Fit
codes.description: IPD enables concurrent design-construction activities, shared risk/reward, joint decision-making, and multiparty contracting, positioning it as best suited to DfMA/off-site/modular delivery, including via CCDC30 in Canada.

codes.label: Manufacturer-Centric Contractual Entities
codes.description: Novel contractual structures (manufacture-builder, manufacture-design-builder) consolidate manufacturing, design and construction responsibility into a single entity to overcome manufacturer isolation in traditional procurement networks.

codes.label: Vertical Integration of Design-Manufacture-Construction
codes.description: Firms are increasingly bringing design, manufacturing, and construction in-house or via joint ventures, redefining traditional contractual boundaries between disciplines.

categories.label: Early Involvement Mechanisms and Timing
categories.memo: Covers specific contractual/procurement mechanisms that enable early engagement of contractors, manufacturers, and suppliers, and the critical timing issues involved.

codes.label: Two-Stage Tendering / ECI Procurement
codes.description: Two-stage tendering and Early Contractor Involvement arrangements allow contractors/suppliers to submit early input or pricing before final design, balancing cost certainty with buildability input; requires careful timing of engagement.

sub_codes.label: Payment for Pre-Construction Services
sub_codes.description: Mechanisms for compensating contractors for pre-construction design input, including no-charge-unless-cancelled arrangements and reimbursement models.','

sub_codes.label: Optimal Timing of Engagement
sub_codes.description: Contractor/manufacturer involvement must occur once sufficient conceptual design exists—too early wastes effort/reduces creativity, too late limits influence on buildability and cost.

codes.label: Alternative Technical Concepts (ATC) Mechanism
codes.description: ATCs allow contractors to propose modifications to contract requirements pre-bid across delivery methods, mitigating risk and enabling innovation, subject to confidentiality and 'equal or better' standards; contractors often unreimbursed for ATC design costs.

codes.label: Design Freeze Requirements
codes.description: MMC/modular projects require early finalization ('design freeze') before fabrication begins, since design changes post-freeze are especially costly and schedule-disruptive, requiring contractual change-control provisions and owner decision timeliness.

codes.label: Preconstruction Services Agreements (PCSA)
codes.description: Supplementary agreements enabling early trade contractor/manufacturer involvement in design development within DBB or CM delivery frameworks to address digital fabrication and constructability needs.

codes.label: Delegation of Administrative/Coordination Burden
codes.description: Because design professionals focus on design perfection, intensive administrative and coordination work in modular/prefab projects should be delegated to construction management firms or separate specialist contracts.

categories.label: Procurement Frameworks and Novel Delivery Models
categories.memo: Covers proposed new or adapted procurement/delivery frameworks specifically tailored to product-based, modular, or off-site manufactured construction, beyond conventional method categories.

codes.label: Product-Based / Product Delivery Models
codes.description: Proposals for treating modular buildings as products with standard supplier contracts including fixed terms and delivery conditions, akin to consumer product transactions, shifting design-rule authority to the modular 'system architect'.

codes.label: Framework/Serial Contracting and Long-Term Partnering
codes.description: Absence of long-term framework or serial tendering arrangements between clients and modular suppliers; proposals for shifting toward fixed long-term partnerships rather than project-by-project procurement.

codes.label: Strategic Partnering and Nominated Suppliers
codes.description: Procurement strategies where owners repeatedly engage reliable suppliers/contractors or nominate suppliers early to facilitate faster, better-planned prefabricated delivery.

codes.label: Separate Contracting for Specialty Precast/Modular Work
codes.description: Owners may mitigate coordination risk by contracting directly and separately with precast/module suppliers or specialty contractors, then engaging a general contractor for remaining work.

codes.label: Selection Criteria for Delivery Method Choice
codes.description: Suitability of a project delivery method for modular construction depends on client profile and characteristics, assessed against multiple selection criteria comparing strengths/weaknesses of PDMs.

categories.label: Multi-Party Coordination, Trust and Relational Governance
categories.memo: Covers how collaboration, trust, and network-based relationships among designers, manufacturers, fabricators, and contractors function as governance mechanisms alongside or instead of formal contract terms.

codes.label: Network Structure vs Linear Supply Chain
codes.description: Prefabrication/timber/OSC supply chains function as networks with feedback loops among design, fabrication and construction actors rather than strictly linear sequences, requiring coordination mechanisms not captured by traditional contract structures.

codes.label: Trust as Complement to Formal Contract Governance
codes.description: Informal relational trust mechanisms emerge to address contractual incompleteness and out-of-contract tasks in OSC projects; contract and trust governance are complementary, with their relative importance shifting across project stages and organizational structures.

codes.label: Vendor/Manufacturer Partnership Agreements
codes.description: Legally nonbinding partnership agreements formalize mutual responsibilities between contractors and manufacturers/vendors regarding communication, delivery, technology and training, functioning as quasi-contractual supply chain governance.

codes.label: Multi-Trade Coordination Requirements
codes.description: Modules combining multiple building systems/trades require increased coordination among subcontractors and suppliers, particularly where no single contractor can perform all necessary work.

codes.label: Manufacturer's Peripheral Power Position in Contract Networks
codes.description: Manufacturers and designers occupy structurally peripheral, low-power positions within common procurement network structures, limiting their influence despite critical roles, while owners retain central control.

codes.label: Collaborative Behavioral Practices under Relational Contracts
codes.description: Alliance and IPD-type contracts require distinct behavioral practices—self-managing teams, open-minded problem resolution, shared pain/gain—that differ from traditional adversarial contracting dynamics.

categories.label: Payment and Financial Structuring Misalignment
categories.memo: Covers how progress payment, valuation, and financing mechanisms in standard/traditional contracts fail to reflect off-site fabrication timing and value, and proposed adaptations.

codes.label: Work-Done vs Work-Due Payment Mismatch
codes.description: Traditional payment provisions tied to on-site work completion conflict with MMC's need for upfront financing and off-site value creation, requiring a shift toward paying for 'work due' rather than 'work done' on site.

codes.label: Ambiguity in Contractual Definitions of 'Products'/Modules
codes.description: Standard contract definitions (e.g., CCDC 'Products') do not clearly encompass prefabricated modules, creating ambiguity about payment claims for fabricated but undelivered or uninstalled modules.

codes.label: Retention and Liquidated Damages Adjustments
codes.description: MMC contract amendments commonly target reduction or removal of retention and liquidated damages provisions to better fit off-site production financial models.

codes.label: Insolvency and Payment Security Risk
codes.description: Insolvency risk among specialist MMC suppliers heightens concern about payment security under existing contract payment structures.

codes.label: Litigation Evidence of Payment Term Disputes
codes.description: Empirical court case analysis shows unclear payment terms are a leading cause of disputes in modular/off-site construction projects, more so than in conventional construction disputes.

categories.label: Sector, Union and Regulatory Constraints on Delivery Method Choice
categories.memo: Covers external structural constraints—labor relations, regulatory frameworks, public procurement rules—that shape which delivery methods and contractual arrangements are viable for MMC/prefabrication.

codes.label: Labor Union Resistance to Prefabrication
codes.description: Union agreements and resistance to outsourced or off-site prefabrication constrain contractors' choice of delivery/procurement models, with differentiated resistance for in-house versus outsourced fabrication.

codes.label: Public Procurement Rules Disadvantaging Innovative MMC Firms
codes.description: Public sector procurement restrictions and local labor/social value requirements favor larger traditional providers over smaller innovative MMC firms, limiting delivery method innovation.

codes.label: Absence of Standard MOC/MMC Contracts and Guidelines
codes.description: Lack of standard contracts specifically for modular/off-site construction (e.g., in Canada) forces adaptation of conventional construction contracts, increasing ambiguity and dispute potential; broader lack of legislative/guideline frameworks impedes systematic adoption.

codes.label: Government Policy and Client Leadership as Adoption Drivers
codes.description: Strong government policy promotion and client leadership are identified as critical drivers enabling adoption of high-rise modular/off-site delivery approaches.

categories.label: Buildability, Design Liability and Risk Allocation across Delivery Methods
categories.memo: Covers how design responsibility, buildability risk, and liability are allocated differently depending on the chosen delivery method, and gaps in addressing MMC-specific risks.

codes.label: Design-Manufacturing Mismatch and Buildability Risk
codes.description: Recurring buildability issues arise from mismatches between design intent and manufacturing/fabrication constraints (e.g., oversized panels, connectivity problems), often not covered by standard physical-conditions relief clauses.

codes.label: Fitness-for-Purpose vs Reasonable Skill and Care Standards
codes.description: Contractors undertaking design responsibility face a higher fitness-for-purpose legal standard compared to consultants' reasonable skill and care standard, significant for allocating buildability risk under design-build/OSM arrangements.

codes.label: Liability Allocation in Digital Fabrication across Delivery Models
codes.description: Different project delivery models (DBB, DB, CM, IPD) allocate liability for digital fabrication errors differently; IPD requires fewer supplementary liability provisions while DBB's fragmentation creates greater liability exposure.

codes.label: Unaddressed Contractual Risk Allocation in MiC/MOC Literature
codes.description: Existing literature and standard forms of contract (FIDIC, NEC, CCDC) have not clearly addressed risk allocation, dispute handling, or suitability assessment specific to MiC/MOC projects, leaving key contractual questions (advance payment, insurance, variation orders) unresolved.

codes.label: Scope, Roles and Responsibility Ambiguity in DfMA Contracts
codes.description: Standard contracts often lack clear definitions of scope of work, stakeholder roles/responsibilities, guarantees/insurance, and references to multiple manufacturers, creating confusion and duplication in DfMA-based delivery.
